notes: Slot 23 = Hashemite royal family (King Hussein). Parties have been banned since 1957, so professional bodies, notables and the security apparatus fill several Western slots. Fatah sits in slot 6, PFLP in 5 and PDFLP (1970 name of the DFLP) in 19; JCP moved from MD slot 19 to 4 (pro-Soviet, has popularity). MD's post-1989 parties (IAF, HASHD, Popular Unity) are anachronistic and were replaced.

0.name: Da'irat al-Mukhabarat al-Amma
0.text:
The General Intelligence Directorate, the Mukhabarat, was created in 1964 under Muhammad Rasul al-Kilani to protect the throne from Nasserist, Ba'athist and communist plots. Trained with British and American help, it has become one of the most effective security services in the region. Since 1967 its main target has been the Palestinian commando organizations that now control whole quarters of Amman.

The Mukhabarat believes that only a firm hand and a close partnership with Washington and London can save the kingdom. It wants the fedayeen disarmed and their leaders expelled. Its leverage is its files, its informers inside every movement and the king's trust.

1.name: Wujaha al-Diffa
1.text:
The West Bank Notables are the mayors, landowners and old families of Hebron, Nablus and Jerusalem who served the Hashemite state from 1950 until the Israeli occupation of June 1967. Men such as Muhammad Ali al-Ja'bari, the mayor of Hebron, and Hikmat al-Masri of Nablus still draw salaries and status from Amman while living under Israeli military rule.

The notables want the West Bank returned to Jordan through diplomacy and American mediation, not guerrilla war. They distrust the fedayeen and the radical left, defend property and family authority and look to the king as their protector. Their leverage is local: patronage, clan networks and the municipal councils of the occupied towns.

2.name: Niqabat al-Muhamin al-Urduniyyin
2.text:
The Jordanian Bar Association was founded in 1950. With all political parties banned since 1957, the lawyers' union and the other professional associations have become the main arena of public life in Jordan. Its elected council speaks for an educated, largely Palestinian middle class in Amman, Irbid and Zarqa.

The lawyers demand the restoration of the 1952 constitution, an end to martial law, legal political parties, free elections and a free press. They defend detained activists in court and support the Palestinian cause, but by lawful means. Their base is lawyers, doctors and engineers. Their leverage is professional prestige and their ability to put the government on trial in public.

3.name: Al-Ittihad al-Amm li-Niqabat al-Ummal
3.english: General Federation of Jordanian Trade Unions
3.native_full: Al-Ittihad al-Amm li-Niqabat al-Ummal fi al-Urdun
3.text:
The General Federation of Jordanian Trade Unions was founded in 1954 and brings together the workers of the phosphate mines, the Zarqa refinery, the railways and the building trades. After the purges of 1957 it is closely supervised by the government, but its locals are full of Palestinian workers who sympathize with the fedayeen and the left.

The Federation calls for higher wages, social insurance, labour protection and the right to strike, and it wants trade unions free of security service interference. It avoids open confrontation with the throne. Its base is the small industrial working class of Amman and Zarqa. Its leverage lies in the phosphate mines and the refinery, which the economy cannot do without.

4.name: Al-Hizb al-Shuyu'i al-Urduni
4.text:
The Jordanian Communist Party was founded in 1951 and has been banned since 1957, when its members were jailed by the hundreds. Fuad Nassar, a veteran of the Palestinian labour movement, is its secretary-general. After long hesitation the party has formed its own armed group, Quwwat al-Ansar, to take part in the resistance.

The JCP follows Moscow closely: it supports the UN Resolution 242 and a political settlement, which puts it at odds with the radical fedayeen. It demands legal political parties, democratic freedoms and land and labour reform. Its base is teachers, students and workers in the West Bank and Amman. Its leverage is discipline and Soviet backing.

5.name: Al-Jabha al-Sha'biyya li-Tahrir Filastin
5.english: Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine
5.text:
The Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine was founded in December 1967 by George Habash, the physician who led the Arab Nationalist Movement. It has its bases in the refugee camps of Amman and Zarqa. Its aircraft hijackings since 1968 have made it world-famous, and Wadie Haddad runs its external operations.

The Front sees the Hashemite monarchy as an obstacle to the liberation of Palestine and openly calls for its overthrow, along with the other reactionary Arab regimes. It is Marxist-Leninist, anti-imperialist and hostile to the United States. Its base is radicalized refugees, students and intellectuals. Its leverage lies in its armed militants and their readiness to provoke a showdown with the army.
5.wiki: Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine

6.name: Fatah
6.text:
Fatah was founded in Kuwait in the late 1950s by Yasser Arafat, Khalil al-Wazir and Salah Khalaf. Since the battle of Karameh in March 1968 it has been the largest commando organization in Jordan, and since February 1969 Arafat has also chaired the Palestine Liberation Organization. Its fighters move armed through Amman, set up roadblocks and collect taxes in the camps.

Fatah stands for the liberation of all Palestine through armed struggle and for Palestinian independence from Arab regimes. It officially avoids interfering in Jordanian affairs, but its presence is creating a state within a state. It is hostile to the West and receives arms from China, the Arab states and increasingly the Soviet bloc. Its leverage is tens of thousands of fighters.

7.name: Hizb al-Ba'th al-Arabi al-Ishtiraki – Qutr al-Urdun
7.english: Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party – Jordan Region
7.native_full: Hizb al-Ba'th al-Arabi al-Ishtiraki – Qutr al-Urdun
7.text:
The Jordanian branch of the Ba'ath Party took part in the nationalist governments of the 1950s and was then outlawed in 1957. Since the Damascus coup of 1966, its pro-Syrian wing takes its line, money and arms from Salah Jadid's regime and works through the As-Sa'iqa commandos stationed in northern Jordan.

The pro-Syrian Ba'ath wants to overthrow the monarchy and bring Jordan into a revolutionary Arab front led from Damascus. It preaches socialism, Arab unity and people's war, and looks to the Soviet Union as an ally. Its base is in Irbid, Ramtha and the northern camps. Its leverage depends on Syrian troops and tanks just across the border.

8.name: Zuwwar al-Mazar
8.text:
The Pilgrims of al-Mazar are the small community of Shia families of Lebanese and Iraqi origin in Amman and Irbid, together with the pilgrims who visit the shrines of Ja'far ibn Abi Talib and the martyrs of Mu'ta near Karak. In a kingdom whose ruling family claims descent from the Prophet, they enjoy quiet tolerance and royal protection.

The community asks for recognition of its own religious courts, freedom of worship and the maintenance of the Mu'ta shrines. It shows loyalty to the Hashemites, whose lineage it respects, and favours the reformist message of Musa al-Sadr in Lebanon. Its leverage is small, resting on trade links with Lebanon and Iraq and the king's goodwill.

9.name: Muhajiru Najaf
9.text:
The Exiles of Najaf are the Iraqi Shia seminarians, merchants and activists who left Iraq after the Ba'athist regime turned on the Najaf seminaries and Grand Ayatollah Muhsin al-Hakim in 1969. A few have found shelter in Amman, where they keep in touch with the clandestine Islamic Dawa movement at home.

The Exiles want rule guided by the senior jurists and the overthrow of the secular Ba'ath in Baghdad. They are hostile to communism and to the Western powers alike. In Jordan they are guests rather than actors, and they depend on the king's rivalry with Baghdad. Their leverage is the network of seminaries stretching from Najaf to Qom and Beirut.

10.name: Al-Awqaf al-Islamiyya fi al-Quds
10.text:
The Jerusalem Islamic Waqf administers the Haram al-Sharif, the al-Aqsa Mosque and the Dome of the Rock under Jordanian authority. Even after the Israeli occupation of East Jerusalem in 1967, it continues to be paid and appointed from Amman. Its ulama and preachers are the official religious voice of the kingdom alongside the Ministry of Awqaf.

The establishment ulama preach loyalty to the Hashemite king as guardian of the holy places, defend Islamic law in personal matters and denounce both atheistic communism and the radicals who threaten order. They keep close ties with Saudi Arabia. Their leverage is the pulpit of al-Aqsa and the religious legitimacy they lend the crown.

11.name: Hizb al-Tahrir
11.text:
Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Islamic Liberation Party, was founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by Taqi al-Din al-Nabhani and is strongest in Jordan and the West Bank. Banned from the start, it has repeatedly tried to win over army officers. In 1968 and 1969 the authorities uncovered coup plots in Amman and arrested dozens of its members.

The party rejects the monarchy, nationalism and all man-made constitutions, and seeks to restore a single caliphate by seizing power through the armed forces. It sees the fedayeen and the Arab regimes alike as distractions. Its members are educated young men from Hebron, Nablus and Amman. Its leverage is its secret cells and its persistence.

12.name: Jama'at al-Ikhwan al-Muslimin
12.text:
The Muslim Brotherhood in Jordan was founded in 1945 and is the only political movement still allowed to operate openly. It is registered as a charitable society and has stood by the throne against the Nasserists and communists since 1957. Muhammad Abd al-Rahman Khalifa has been its general supervisor since 1953.

The Brotherhood calls for the application of Islamic law, religious education and moral reform, and supports the jihad for Palestine through its own small commando camps. It is anti-communist and wary of the leftist fedayeen. Its base is teachers, merchants and the pious middle class of Amman, Salt and the camps. Its leverage is its legal status, schools and mosques.

13.name: Rijal al-Diwan
13.text:
The Men of the Royal Court are the palace advisers, cabinet ministers and senior civil servants who actually run the kingdom from day to day. Their leading figure is Prime Minister Bahjat al-Talhouni, a seasoned court politician who seeks to contain the fedayeen through negotiation and compromise rather than force.

The Court men believe in careful balance: between East Bank and West Bank, between the army hardliners and the Palestinian organizations, and between Washington and the Arab states that pay Jordan's subsidies. They avoid ideology and serve the crown. Their leverage is administration, appointments and their direct access to King Hussein.

14.name: Shuyukh al-Badiya
14.text:
The Sheikhs of the Badia are the leaders of the great Bedouin tribes of the East Bank, such as the Bani Sakhr and the Huwaytat, whose sons fill the ranks of the army. Akif al-Fayez of the Bani Sakhr, a minister and member of parliament, is the most prominent of them. They have been the backbone of the Hashemite throne since the founding of the emirate.

The sheikhs stand for tribal honour, Islamic tradition, loyalty to the king and the privileges of the East Bank. They resent the armed fedayeen who insult soldiers at checkpoints and demand that the army be allowed to restore order. Their leverage is the loyalty of the Bedouin regiments.

15.name: Al-Bank al-Arabi
15.text:
The Arab Bank was founded in Jerusalem in 1930 by Abdul Hameed Shoman and moved its headquarters to Amman after 1948. It is the largest private financial institution in the Arab world, with branches from Beirut to the Gulf. Around it gather the Palestinian and Jordanian merchant and contracting families who finance the kingdom's economy.

The bankers and merchants want stability, open trade, investment and good relations with both the Gulf states and the West. They quietly fund Palestinian institutions while dreading a civil war that would ruin their business. Their leverage is enormous: the state, the commando organizations and the refugee economy all depend on their money.

16.name: Ghurfat Tijarat Amman
16.text:
The Amman Chamber of Commerce was founded in 1923 and represents the shopkeepers, importers and traders of a capital that has grown from a town into a city of half a million in a single generation. Its members, many of them Palestinian, Syrian and Circassian, are the face of Jordan's market economy.

The merchants want low duties, free movement of goods across the Jordan bridges and to Beirut, little state interference and an end to commando taxes and roadblocks in the city's streets. They reject the socialist experiments of Damascus and Cairo. Their leverage is the commerce of the capital, which can bring Amman to a standstill with a strike.

17.name: Al-Jam'iyya al-Malakiyya li-Himayat al-Tabi'a
17.english: Royal Society for the Conservation of Nature
17.text:
The Royal Society for the Conservation of Nature was founded in 1966 under the patronage of King Hussein. It was the first conservation body in the Arab world. It began with a campaign against uncontrolled hunting, which has driven the Arabian oryx and the gazelle to the edge of extinction in the Jordanian desert.

The Society calls for hunting laws, protected reserves in the Azraq oasis and Shaumari, reforestation of the northern highlands and careful use of Jordan's scarce water. It works with Western conservation groups and enjoys royal favour. Its base is educated Ammanis, army officers who hunt and foreign experts. Its leverage is royal patronage.
17.wiki: Royal Society for the Conservation of Nature

18.name: Al-Hizb al-Watani al-Ishtiraki
18.text:
The National Socialist Party was founded in 1954 by Sulayman al-Nabulsi and won the free elections of 1956, forming Jordan's only elected nationalist government. It abrogated the treaty with Britain, but in April 1957 the king dismissed Nabulsi and banned all parties. Nabulsi lives in Amman, respected and closely watched.

The party stands for constitutional monarchy, free elections, Arab unity, neutrality between the blocs and moderate socialist reform. It supports the Palestinian resistance while hoping to avoid a war between the army and the fedayeen. Its base is the urban middle class and veteran nationalists of Salt, Nablus and Amman. Its leverage is Nabulsi's prestige as a democratic alternative.

19.name: Al-Jabha al-Sha'biyya al-Dimuqratiyya li-Tahrir Filastin
19.english: Popular Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine
19.text:
The Popular Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine split from the PFLP in February 1969 under Nayef Hawatmeh, a Jordanian Christian from Salt. It is the most theoretical of the commando groups, and its cadres read Lenin, Mao and Giap in the camps of Amman and the Jordan valley.

The Front calls for a people's war and the transformation of Jordan into a revolutionary base: 'all power to the resistance'. It supports councils of workers and peasants and an independent Marxist line, critical of both Moscow and the Arab regimes. Its base is students and young refugees. Its leverage lies in its armed militias and its influence on the radical left across the Arab world.
19.wiki: Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine

20.name: Ansar Wasfi
20.text:
Wasfi's Partisans are the East Bank officials, officers and tribal politicians who gather around Wasfi al-Tal, the former prime minister and the most outspoken enemy of the commando state. Out of office but close to the king, Tal argues that the kingdom must decide who rules in Amman before the fedayeen decide for it.

The Partisans stand for Jordanian sovereignty, the authority of the army and an East Bank identity distinct from the Palestinian movement. They want the commandos disarmed, Nasserist and leftist agitation crushed and the alliance with the West preserved. Their base is the East Bank bureaucracy, the officer corps and Ajlun and Salt. Their leverage is Tal's reputation and the army's growing anger.

21.name: Hizb al-Ba'th – Tanzim al-Qiyada al-Qawmiyya
21.native_full: Hizb al-Ba'th al-Arabi al-Ishtiraki – Qutr al-Urdun
21.text:
The pro-Iraqi Ba'athists of Jordan remained loyal to Michel Aflaq's National Command after the 1966 split, and since 1968 they have been directed and financed by the Ba'athist regime in Baghdad. Their armed wing is the Arab Liberation Front, founded in April 1969. They benefit from the Iraqi expeditionary force stationed in Jordan since the 1967 war.

The pro-Iraqi Ba'ath wants the overthrow of the monarchy and Jordan's absorption into a revolutionary Arab state led by its party. It preaches unity, socialism and a disciplined single party, and it considers Damascus a usurper. Its base is small but armed. Its leverage is Iraqi money and troops on Jordanian soil.

22.name: Al-Quwwat al-Musallaha al-Urduniyya – al-Jaysh al-Arabi
22.text:
The Jordan Armed Forces, still proudly called the Arab Army, descend from the British-led Arab Legion. They lost the West Bank in 1967, but held at Karameh in 1968. Hardline commanders such as the king's uncle Sharif Nasser bin Jamil and Zaid bin Shaker command its Bedouin-dominated regiments.

The officer corps is loyal to the crown, conservative and increasingly furious at the humiliations heaped on it by the fedayeen. It wants permission to clear the commandos from Amman and the towns and to restore the authority of the state. It is equipped by Britain and the United States. Its leverage is decisive: in any showdown, the army is the kingdom.

23.name: Al-Usra al-Hashimiyya
23.text:
The Hashemite Royal Family descends from the Sharifs of Mecca who led the Arab Revolt of 1916. It has ruled Transjordan and then Jordan since 1921. King Hussein bin Talal has reigned since 1953, survived coup plots and assassination attempts, and now faces the gravest challenge of his reign: armed Palestinian organizations that defy his authority in his own capital.

The monarchy stands for a moderate, Western-aligned Arab state, the recovery of the West Bank and Jerusalem through diplomacy based on UN Resolution 242, and the unity of the two banks under the crown. Its base is the army, the tribes and the East Bank establishment. Its leverage is the king's personal authority.
